title: No room (Luke 2:1–7)
hookLine: a census, a long road, and a baby laid in an animal's feeding trough
carry: God arrived in a feeding trough

cards: Luke opens with an emperor far away signing an order: "And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed." A census, so everyone can be taxed.

Historians still argue about exactly which census Luke means. In a small town in Galilee, a carpenter has to pack up. Joseph belongs to David's family, so he goes south to Bethlehem, David's old town.
And he takes Mary, who is, in the old words, great with child. No donkey is mentioned; Luke just says they went. And while they're there, the days are accomplished.

teach.b: Luke tells the birth in one sentence: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn."
No star, no angels yet, no ox and no donkey.

teach.h: A MANGER IS A FEEDING TROUGH.
teach.b: A manger is a feeding trough; Luke's Greek word is phatne. And there's a clue about the room. The word translated "inn" turns up later in Luke for the guest room where Jesus eats his last supper.

teach.h: A FULL HOUSE, NOT A RUDE INN?
teach.b: So some scholars picture not a hotel with a rude innkeeper, but a crowded family house with the guest room already full, and the animals brought in at night to the lower part of the house, trough and all.

teach.h: THE OX, THE DONKEY, AND FRANCIS.
teach.b: The ox and the donkey come later, from Christians reading an old line in Isaiah: the ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's crib. Crib, in that old English, means the manger.
And near the end of his life, Bonaventure's life of him says, Francis of Assisi set up a manger with a real ox and donkey at Greccio, in Italy, so ordinary people could see it.
Tradition traces the nativity scene back to that night. Some see the humility of God: the one they call the Word made flesh, laid where the animals eat.
In Orthodox icons of the birth, the manger often looks like a small stone tomb, and the swaddling bands like grave cloths, a hint of how the story ends. The emperor gets the first line.

teach.h: GOD ARRIVED IN A FEEDING TROUGH.

how: Many Christian homes and churches set up a nativity scene at Christmas, a custom often traced to Francis of Assisi at Greccio, and many churches read Luke 2 aloud on Christmas Eve.

games.why: Luke says she wrapped him in swaddling clothes and laid him in a manger, because there was no room for them in the inn.

practice: Think of your day as a house with every room already full: plans, errands, the people you expect.
Picture one small space cleared for whatever turns up: a stranger's question, a child who wants to show you something, a slow conversation.
If you pray, offer that space as a place for God; if you don't, just leave it empty, on purpose.

wordCard.voice: Manger. A feeding trough for animals, and, in Luke, the first bed Jesus had, because there was no room.

orig.note: Greek: a manger, a feeding trough, sometimes the stall around it. Luke uses it three times in the birth story.

carryVoice: Your line: God arrived in a feeding trough. Of all the beds, that one. That's forty-one.
